note:
This section introduces the workings of the Persian Empire and makes clear its vast extent and massive resources. However, the conduct of the king is presented as arbitrary and somewhat incompetent.

**1:1–22** The anger the king displays against Vashti and her disappearance from the royal court sets the scene for Esther to become queen, and thus to be in a position to influence the affairs of the empire for the benefit of her people.

**1:1 Ahasuerus.** Also known as Xerxes (486–465 B.C.), Ahasuerus is the Persian king mentioned in Ezra 4:6. He is renowned for consolidating his father Darius’s empire, for his successful building projects, and for his wars against the Greeks from 480 to 470 B.C.

**India.** The area watered by the Indus River, in modern-day Pakistan.

**Ethiopia.** Heb. “Cush,” the region south of Egypt, now part of northern Sudan (see 1 Chr. 1:8). No mention is made of the northern or western boundary where Ahasuerus failed to fully conquer the Greeks.

**127 provinces.** The reference here to the large number of divisions within the thirty larger administrative districts, or satrapies, in the Persian Empire is intended to impress.

This acropolis is a fortified palace 120 feet (36 m) above the surrounding city of Susa, which is the most significant of the four Persian capital cities and the royal winter residence. It has been excavated several times since 1851.
The year is 483 B.C. About this time, Ahasuerus is planning his forthcoming invasion of Greece, which may account for the large military presence in the capital.

For 180 days, the king ostentatiously displays the royal wealth. The extravagant, seven-day outdoor feast is the climax of the celebrations. The elaborate details about the drinking vessels and the abundance of the wine highlight the king’s lavish generosity. All is intended to impress and intimidate, but events will show where control really lies.

This term is employed nineteen times in Esther to refer to royal decrees. Micromanipulation of conduct is characteristic of bureaucracies, ancient and modern. Here the concession is made that each individual is free to drink as much or as often as he pleases.

This name, not found elsewhere, may be related to the Persian word meaning “the beloved” or “the best.” Extrabiblical sources name Ahasuerus’s queen as Amestris. Vashti may have been a popular or an alternative name. Another proposal is that Ahasuerus had other queens.

Reasons for Vashti’s disobedience are not given in the Hebrew text, though early Jewish interpreters explained that she was commanded to appear naked, wearing only her crown, or that she had some disfigurement. The queen’s courageous refusal to obey introduces the theme of obedience and disobedience. The weakness of the regime has been exposed from within, from the top—and by a woman. That a woman would show the regime’s weakness is ironic considering the lower place of women in the eyes of the culture of that day.

This expression usually refers to astrology, though in this context it probably means “the proper course to follow” (see 1 Chr. 12:32). The satirical flavor of the narrative is evident as the king, who has just displayed all the power and glory of his magnificent kingdom, proves incapable of formulating a response to this affront to his self-esteem and has to consult experts on matters of law and justice and to go to the nobles for advice on how to deal with his wife’s behavior.

**the seven princes of Persia and Media.** The king’s inner circle of advisors (see Ezra 7:14). 14

The counselor (as well as the king, v. 10) is probably somewhat intoxicated after the extended banquet. He exaggerates the situation, deftly avoids the king’s role in the affair, and proposes a disproportionate and unenforceable response, which gives massive exposure to the whole incident.

verse_quote: laws of the Persians ... may not be repealed.
note: The permanency of royal law is an important feature in the development of the story (4:11; 8:8). The plan to banish Vashti and to give her position to someone better—more beautiful or more obedient (or both)—has be carried out. The legal structures of the empire are brought into operation to ensure that defiance does not spread.
This is more a piece of court flattery than concern with the difficulties of communication.

verse_quote: letters to all the royal provinces.
note:
The Persian postal system, renowned for its efficiency, is used to publish the irrevocable royal edicts (3:12–14; 8:9, 10; see 9:20, 30).

**master in his own household.** Indeed, the biblical standard is that the husband is the head of the household, but he must exercise his authority in the right spirit: not a display of domineering bullying but of care and love modeled on that of Christ (Eph. 5:22–25).

Steps are taken to replace the deposed Vashti (vv. 1–4). Then Mordecai and Esther are introduced (vv. 5–7). Esther is one of many young women coerced into the process of selecting a new queen (vv. 8–11). Details of the procedure (vv. 12–14) lead into an account of how Ahasuerus is captivated and overwhelmed by Esther (vv. 15–18). Around this time, Mordecai becomes aware of a plot against the king, which his information helps to foil. He does not, however, receive any immediate reward (vv. 19–21).

**2:1 After these things.** Combining the information in vv. 12, 16 with that in 1:3 suggests that approximately three years have past, during which time Ahasuerus was away from Susa, fighting the Greeks (482–480 B.C.).

**abated.** The use of the same rare verb in 7:10 suggests a parallel between the dismissal of Vashti and the hanging of Haman.

**he remembered Vashti.** The king may have regretted his actions, but it was too late; the legislation made his actions permanent.

Probably his personal assistants, not the senior advisors of 1:13, 14. If Ahasuerus does indeed regret deposing Vashti, he may be uninterested in listening to those who suggested it.

**be sought out.** This is not a competition that one chooses to enter but a commandeering exercise on the part of the empire to acquire whatever it wants, no matter the human cost involved.
For the unsuccessful young women it will lead to a life of widowhood, imprisoned in the royal harem.

A name derived from Marduk, the Babylonian city-god. Mordecai may also have a Jewish name, like Esther (Hadassah, v. 7). The discovery in ancient texts (including one dated c. 485 B.C.) of the Babylonian personal name Mardukaya, as well as the discovery of an archive of texts in Nippur containing the names of Jews from the time of Artaxerxes I and Darius, point to the authenticity of Mordecai’s name and to the historicity of the events behind the story. Mordecai was a Jew living in the citadel, which presumably implies that he was a Persian official.

**Jair ... Shimei ... Kish.** The names in his genealogy may refer to Mordecai’s remote rather than immediate ancestors (Shimei, 2 Sam. 16:5–14; Kish, 1 Sam. 9:1, 2; 1 Chr. 8:33). Kish may well have been an earlier ancestor rather than the one carried into exile, who in that case would be Jair. The reference is not to Mordecai personally—that would have made him about 120 years old. Mordecai’s connection with Saul, who was also a Benjaminite, takes on great significance when we encounter Haman, Mordecai’s enemy, who was a distant relative of Agag, the Amalekite, Saul’s enemy (3:1 note; Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

Also known as Jehoiachin, the second-to-last king of Judah, who was taken to Babylon in 597 B.C. while still a young man. This may mean that Mordecai’s family was among the Judean nobility (2 Kin. 24:6–17; 25:27–30).

Esther’s Hebrew name, meaning “myrtle.”

**Esther.** Perhaps derived from the Persian word for “star,” or a form of Ishtar, a Babylonian goddess. The family information given shows that Esther was not Mordecai’s niece but his cousin. Since Esther became his adopted daughter, she was presumably younger than Mordecai.
This brings out the initial vulnerability of Esther. She had no option in the matter.

A secular use of the Hebrew word for “covenant loyalty,” _hesed_ (Ex. 15:13 note). The idiom is normally used with the more passive verb “found” (e.g., Gen. 39:4); the active verb “won” suggests that Esther took advantage of the opportunities in her new situation. Hegai’s attitude is also a first sign of God’s providential care of Esther (see v. 17; 5:2; cf. the more explicit references to God’s providence in Dan. 1:9). Hegai’s speedy arrangements and provision of the “best place in the harem” mark Esther as the woman most likely to succeed in the selection process.

**her portion of food.** Esther’s reception of special portions of food contrasts with her intentional fast in 4:16. Life in the harem is highly regulated, as in the empire as a whole. Unlike Daniel, Esther does not follow Jewish dietary laws or declare her background (v. 10).
The elaborate preparations are in keeping with the other excesses of the court (1:4–8).
The place reserved for concubines, the king’s mistresses.
**the tenth month ... the seventh year.** Corresponds to December 479/January 478 B.C., four years after 1:3.

verse_quote: he set the royal crown on her head.
note: Ahasuerus is completely captivated by Esther and makes her queen immediately.

Esther’s accession to the throne, which is celebrated with a banquet, contrasts with Vashti’s banquet in 1:9.

**a remission.** Lit. “a giving of rest.” Perhaps a declaration of a public holiday, but remission of taxes is attested as a royal concession in the Persian Empire. This, along with giving gifts (probably food) and other favors, foreshadows the great banquet and rest for the Jews in 9:16–18, 22. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

It is unclear what this refers to; perhaps a second selection of a concubine or part of the celebrations at Esther’s feast.

**at the king’s gate.** This expression (see v. 21; 3:2; 5:9, 13; 6:10, 12) may imply that Mordecai has been promoted in the royal service, a move that not only enables him to discover the conspiracy to assassinate the king (v. 21) but which also may be what incites Haman’s jealousy (5:13). The king’s gate is a large structure that houses key elements of the royal administration. Sitting there does not depict the attitude of a bystander or a supplicant but of a court official.
These personal bodyguards control access to the king’s private quarters and so have easy access to him.

Lit. “on a tree.” Refers to impalement on a wooden stake, a Persian and Assyrian form of execution. To the Jews, this is a sign that the two officials are under God’s curse (Deut. 21:22, 23 and note), confirming the appropriateness of Mordecai’s loyalty to the pagan king.

**recorded in the book of the chronicles.** Mordecai is not rewarded at this time (see 6:1–11); instead, the account of Haman’s promotion is given (3:1). Since Persian kings were usually scrupulous in rewarding exceptional service, the fact that the king grants no prize to Mordecai in this instance demonstrates God’s providential control. Ahasuerus’s failure to reward Mordecai at this point allows the king to reward him later, providing evidence of God’s overruling Haman’s wicked plans in order to bring about the evil man’s downfall (Est. 6:1–13).

A crisis is precipitated as events take a threatening turn. Unexpectedly and with no explanation stated, Ahasuerus promotes Haman (not Mordecai, as 2:22 might lead the reader to expect) to second position in the empire. However, Haman and Mordecai are soon found opposing each other (vv. 1–6). Haman abuses his position of trust to dupe Ahasuerus into promulgating a decree of genocide against the Jews (vv. 7–14). Again Ahasuerus is portrayed in a poor light as he makes decisions without securing adequate information.

**3:1 After these things.** The precise time lapse from 2:17 depends on one’s understanding of 3:7. Four, or more probably five, years have now passed.

**Haman the Agagite.** The antagonist of this story bears the Persian name _Haman_ and is the son of the Persian _Hammedatha_, but the true significance of the man is found in the identification of Haman as “the Agagite.” This suggests that Haman has an important association with Agag, the king of the Amalekites, the archenemies of Israel, who were opposed by Saul (1 Sam. 14:47–15:35). God called on the ancestors of Mordecai and Esther to blot out the Amalekites, and the presence of one of them in the days of Esther shows that the job remains unfinished (Ex. 17:8–16; Deut. 25:17–19). Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin, failed to obey God immediately and kill Agag. Now, Esther and Mordecai, also from the tribe of Benjamin, are left to deal with his descendant.

verse_quote: Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage.
note: Mordecai’s refusal to honor Haman cannot be explained on the basis of OT law, since Jews do not regard bowing before kings and other honored persons as a violation of the first and second commandments (Ex. 20:3–6; 1 Sam. 25:23; 2 Sam. 18:28; 2 Kin. 4:37). Mordecai and Haman are best understood as representatives of two hostile nations—Israel and its enemy Amalek, a nation under the divine curse (v. 1 note), respectively. Mordecai’s refusal to bow down to his hereditary enemy because he (Mordecai) “was a Jew” is understandable (v. 4). Similarly, Haman’s seemingly excessive passion to destroy the entire Jewish nation for Mordecai’s insolence is explained (v. 6). Ultimately, this hostility is a particular manifestation of that divinely imposed conflict between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent in Gen. 3:15.

verse_quote: he had told them that he was a Jew.
note: It is strange that only at this point does Mordecai take a stand, since there are many other objectionable features of life in the royal court in Susa. Still, a late stand is better than no stand at all.
“Fury” is the same word translated “anger” (1:12; 2:1). Haman shares the character trait with Ahasuerus. Indeed, there is a play on how similar the name Haman sounds in Hebrew to “fury” (_hemah_).

Haman’s vehement passion will not stop at half-measures in seeking revenge. He will deal not simply with Mordecai but with his whole race. So the continuation of the covenantal line of promise that is to produce the Messiah comes under threat, as the Persians control the lives even of those Jews who have already returned to Jerusalem.

Haman uses the ancient practice of casting lots (1 Sam. 14:41, 42; Prov. 16:33) to determine the most propitious time to set in motion his plan to destroy the Jews. The lots probably take the form of small clay cubes. The plural form of _Pur_—_Purim_—is the name of the celebration that commemorates the death of Haman, the enemy of all the Jews (9:23–32).

**they cast it month after month.** There are two understandings of what is related here. (1) The process of casting lots takes place daily for almost a year (475 B.C.). (2) More probably, on one day in the first month of the year (early April 474 B.C.) lots are cast for each month and day in succession until the last month of the year emerges as propitious. This, too, is part of the Lord’s providence to allow time for the deliverance of His people. Haman is prepared to endure that delay to ensure the success of his scheme, but he approaches the king immediately to set his plan in motion.

Haman’s speech is a calculated blend of truth (“scattered abroad and dispersed”) and falsehood (“they do not keep the king’s laws”). If Mordecai and Esther are anything to go by, the Jews are largely prepared to assimilate. Without naming the Jews, Haman uses vague and unsubstantiated allegations to imply that they threaten to be a disruptive influence in the empire.

**3:9 10,000 talents of silver.** This enormous bribe is calculated at about two-thirds the annual revenue of the Persian Empire under King Darius. Ahasuerus asks no questions, but quickly accepts Haman’s offer, probably because he has been depleted by his earlier generosity (2:18) and his unsuccessful war against the Greeks.

Yet another of the king’s impulsive responses authorizes Haman to issue royal edicts (see Gen. 41:42). The repetition of Haman’s full name together with the phrase “the enemy of the Jews” underlines the terrible predicament of the Jews at this point. Haman has been able to manipulate the king with ease.

verse_quote: The money is given to you.
note: The king is not refusing Haman’s offer. It seems to be understood that Haman will recoup this enormous expense by appropriating the assets of those killed. The king is authorizing him to do so—and expects the promised payment to the royal treasury (see 4:7).

The impersonal imperial administrative machine swings into action to process Haman’s plans. The elaborate, descriptive language (e.g., the multiple verbs in the edict “to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate”) highlights the painfulness of the senseless edict and emphasizes the extreme danger to God’s covenant people. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

**3:12 the thirteenth day of the first month.** The significance of this day—the eve of the Passover celebration—would not be lost on any Jew. Now it would not be a commemoration of divine deliverance but the start of an ominous shadow cast over the Jews. It has been calculated to correspond to April 17, 474 B.C.

On March 7, 473 B.C., almost a full year later.

**to plunder their goods.** To be compared with the Jews’ refusal to plunder (9:10, 15, 16).

verse_quote: the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
note: While the king and Haman callously feast, the city, not just the administrative classes in the citadel, is in a highly agitated state. There is probably a measure of sympathy for the Jews, but equally there is surely bewilderment as to what the future might hold for other people groups as a result of Haman’s influence over the emperor.

The royal decree issued as a result of Haman’s plot plunges the Jewish community, near and far, into deep mourning (vv. 1–3). Esther becomes aware of the threat to the Jews only through the information passed on by Mordecai. Then the initiative in events moves from the king and his courtiers, first to Mordecai and then to Esther. Mordecai orders Esther to approach the king to induce him to intervene in the situation (vv. 4–9). After Esther sets out the difficulties involved in his proposal (vv. 10, 11), Mordecai warns her that her life too is in danger (vv. 12–14). Esther then prepares to act, hazarding her personal safety (vv. 15–17).

**4:1 all that had been done.** Mordecai keeps himself well-informed about what goes on in court. His knowledge is not confined to the public decree. He has insider information.

**4:1–3 tore his clothes ... bitter cry ... fasting ... ashes.** These responses by Mordecai and by Jews in every province are conventional signs of intense grief and horror at the reception of bad news in a society that does not despise public displays of emotion (see Gen. 37:29, 34; Dan. 9:3; Jon. 3:6). The Persians responded similarly after their defeat by the Greeks at the battle of Salamis.

**sackcloth.** Rough garments, often of goats’ hair, worn in mourning or distress.

Esther’s life in the palace has become so detached from the rest of her people that she does not know about the decree and the danger they are in. But she does know that Mordecai’s action indicates that something is very much amiss. Her initial concern is for Mordecai personally.
His name may mean “the good one,” or perhaps “courier.” He certainly acts in a trustworthy manner.

See 3:12–14. Mordecai makes sure that Esther not only is given a copy of the edict but also has it explained to her (perhaps translated) before he charges her to entreat the king for mercy for her people. Mordecai’s previous command that Esther conceal her identity as a Jew is reversed (2:10).
Persian kings live under perpetual fear of assassination, and this practice gives clear direction to the royal bodyguards as to how to deal with an unexpected visitor.

Mordecai subtly alludes to his belief that God, in His sovereignty, has providentially ordered the events of Esther’s life to put her in a position where she can act to deliver all the Jews. Mordecai believes that the sovereign God will bring relief and deliverance to the Jews, that Esther could be the means through which that deliverance will come, and that God is not restricted to this plan if Esther decides to remain quiet. However, it is striking that Mordecai manages to communicate those things without directly mentioning the Lord’s name once.

Esther now takes the lead in shaping the response to the crisis (see Mordecai’s compliance in v. 17).

**Go, gather ... fast on my behalf.** With conviction, faith, and fear, Esther directs that a fast be undertaken on her behalf. Prayer normally accompanies religious fasting (Deut. 9:9; Judg. 20:26, 27; 2 Sam. 12:16; Ezra 8:21–23; Dan. 9:3) but is left out here. However, fasting itself contains an implicit appeal to God to save His people from destruction.

**three days, night or day.** Usually, fasts are prescribed for only one day. This unusually long fast points to the seriousness of the situation and effectively contrasts with the feasts that stand at the beginning and end of the book (1:3, 5, 9; 2:18; 9:17, 18).

**against the law.** See v. 8. Esther’s dilemma reintroduces the theme of obedience, since obedience to Mordecai means disobeying the law of the land.

**if I perish, I perish.** Given Ahasuerus’s temper, there is a significant possibility that he will not accept her. Yet in obedience to Mordecai’s request, Esther resigns herself to her fate (see Gen. 43:14).

The scene switches from the bleak world outside to the splendor of the court, from the fasting of the Jews to the feasting of the palace. After she overcomes the initial hurdle of an audience with Ahasuerus, Esther cautiously and successfully manipulates events to achieve her purpose.

**5:1** Wearing royal robes that undoubtedly enhance her beauty (cf. the mourning attire in 4:15, 16), Esther dares to approach the threshold of the imperial throne room. To emphasize that Esther is entering another world, the narrator repeats the word “king” three times and the word “royal” twice.
Ahasuerus grants Esther’s request for an audience. The immediate threat to her life has been removed, but the situation remains far from resolution.

This generous offer reflects a courtly convention and should not be taken literally (v. 6; see Mark 6:23). Esther’s first request is that the king and Haman attend a banquet (v. 4). Her second response (v. 8) effectively obliges the king to grant her petition. But it is not until 7:2–6 that Esther finally answers the king’s question. Esther’s delaying tactics not only demonstrate her wisdom and sense of control but also raise the suspense in the story.
Esther does not move too fast. The inclusion of Haman would occasion no surprise due to his recent promotion.

Esther’s second response effectively obliges Ahasuerus to grant her petition, but it is not until 7:2–6 that Esther reveals what that is. Subtly, she makes the second banquet seem like the king’s idea.

Haman’s elation at the honor extended to him as the only guest at an intimate meal with Ahasuerus and his queen is shattered when he again witnesses Mordecai’s defiant attitude toward him (v. 9). At a gathering of family and friends to boast about his status (vv. 10–12), Haman reveals his irritation with Mordecai. His wife and friends advise him to use his influence with the king to have Mordecai eliminated (v. 14).

**5:9 filled with wrath.** The same expression as “filled with fury” (3:5). Mordecai has evidently removed his sackcloth and is back at his post.
Though infuriated, Haman unexpectedly does not openly react to Mordecai’s snub and pretends not to notice it.
Haman does not give details of what has happened but makes his vexation with Mordecai clear.

Haman was content to leave Mordecai’s fate to be determined by the general decree against the Jews (3:6), but now his wife and friends urge him to act immediately against Mordecai.

**fifty cubits high.** Whether hanging or impalement is in view, the height of about seventy-five feet (23 m) is excessive (but then, so was much else connected with the Persian court). Possibly the gallows is to be erected on top of something else so that Mordecai’s demise will be a public spectacle.

**Then go joyfully.** The ruthless policy of arranging a political assassination so that he can enjoy a banquet and his new status at court appeals to Haman.

This chapter constitutes the watershed in the narrative. Events begin to turn around for the people of God through a striking series of events, each plausible when considered in isolation, but their combination reveals the working of a higher hand. The king has a bout of insomnia (v. 1). He is reminded that Mordecai has never received any reward (vv. 2, 3). Even though it is still night, Ahas­uerus calls for a royal advisor (v. 4). Haman is in attendance because he is eager to have Mordecai executed (v. 5). Haman, thinking the conversation is about himself, advises the king how to honor a favorite courtier (vv. 6–9). But, far from receiving the accolade himself, Haman is ordered to bestow it on Mordecai (vv. 10, 11). Utterly frustrated and humiliated, Haman returns home (vv. 12, 13).

**6:1 the king could not sleep.** Lit. “the sleep of the king fled,” but we are not told why. The hand of God is at work. The chronicles of eastern kings are tedious, but the intention is probably to induce the king to sleep.

There does not seem to have been any particular reason to read the account of a five-year-old conspiracy (see 2:19–23). Again the hand of God is at work. To enhance their personal safety, Persian monarchs richly rewarded informers (see 2:23), and Ahasuerus is perturbed that Mordecai has been overlooked.

He has spent the night supervising the construction of the gallows for Mordecai, so ironically he is there at dawn to request Mordecai’s death just as the king is seeking advice on how to honor Mordecai.

In a further ironic turn, the king—unintentionally—does not reveal the identity of the one to be honored (see Haman’s intentional concealment of the identity of the people to be destroyed, 3:8). Assuming that he himself is the focus of the king’s favor, Haman unveils his personal dream list, which focuses not on material gain or position but on public acclaim and adulation (see Gen. 41:42, 43). He wants to be treated as if he were king and for all Susa to know about it.
Though Ahasuerus has no idea of the hostility between the two men, others are likely well aware of it.

verse_quote: through the square of the city.
note: Just days before, Mordecai was there wearing sackcloth (4:2).
A deliberate contrast between Mordecai’s returning to his post and Haman’s returning home utterly dejected and forlorn.

Haman’s wife and advisors give voice to the belief that the Jewish people are indomitable and, perhaps, even to the view that their God is the living God. See the predictions about the fall of Amalek before Israel (Ex. 17:16; Num. 24:20; Deut. 25:17–19; 1 Sam. 15; 2 Sam. 1:8–16; cf. predictions of others fearing God’s people and the Lord in Josh. 2:11; Dan. 6:26, 27; Ezek. 38:23). See also Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

The pace quickens. Haman is hurried to the banquet before he has time to think (6:14). On this occasion, Esther reveals the plight of her people (vv. 3, 4) and denounces Haman as the would-be perpetrator of genocide (v. 6). Haman’s attempt to win a reprieve from the queen is misinterpreted by Ahasuerus (vv. 7, 8), and Haman is sentenced to die on the gallows he has prepared personally (vv. 9, 10).

**6:14 hurried to bring Haman.** The affairs of the court are always carried out in haste. It was oriental custom for servants to escort guests to special functions. Events have spun out of Haman’s control; Esther is now in charge.

As on the first occasion (5:5) wine is drunk after the banquet (5:6).

**Queen Esther.** Ahasuerus’s use of her title here (as in 5:3) indicates his favorable disposition toward her. The title is also used in vv. 1, 3, 5 and 7, emphasizing her dominant role in this scene.

The drama of the scene is heightened by Esther’s slow unveiling of her twofold petition for her own life and for her people to be spared, corresponding to the king’s twofold offer to grant her wish and her request (v. 2). Esther does not name her people, but the fate awaiting them makes her nationality obvious.

A reference to Haman’s initial bribe (3:9; 4:7).

**destroyed ... killed ... annihilated.** The Hebrew verbs are precisely those used in the initial decree (3:13). Esther identifies with her people but does not yet come completely into the open. She skillfully uses passive verbs in her description to avoid implicating the king.

**not to be compared.** The Hebrew is somewhat difficult to translate. Esther seems to argue that Haman’s financial offer (3:9) will not compensate for the king’s damages (i.e., lost revenue from the Jews). Appealing to Ahasuerus’s self-interest is virtually certain to sway him.

Esther’s tactics have completely won over the king. When he angrily demands to be told who has threatened the queen and her people, Esther makes no mention of the king’s own decree but points to Haman as the instigator of the genocidal atrocity. “Foe” and “enemy” point not just to hostility to Esther and her people but to Ahasuerus’s interests as well.

**terrified.** Haman is gripped with sudden, overwhelming fear as he realizes that there is no way out. The king and queen are united in opposing him., 6

It is improbable that Ahasuerus wants a place to cool off. Though Esther has not named him personally, the decree went out with his authority, and the whole situation reflects badly on him. He needs time to work out how to extricate himself without losing face.

It is the custom to recline on couches at a feast in this era. Haman’s violations of etiquette seal his fate and provide Ahasuerus with a neat way out of the tricky situation he finds himself in.

**covered Haman’s face.** The court attendants understand the implications of the king’s word, that is, his verdict regarding Haman’s guilt.

As always, the king welcomes the advice of others—here, the eunuch Harbona (1:10; see the speech in 5:14). The order to hang Haman on the gallows intended for Mordecai is the great ironic reversal of the story. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes., 10

Though Haman, the main adversary of the Jews, has been removed from the scene, the story is not over. The edict to annihilate the Jews is still in place with all the inescapable fixity of the laws of the Medes and Persians. Esther again approaches the king (v. 3) and asks for the law to be revoked (v. 5). Ahasuerus gives Esther and Mordecai permission to proceed as they think best (v. 8), and Mordecai formulates a decree (v. 9) that effectively counters the impact of Haman’s edict by authorizing the Jews to take action against any who attack them (vv. 11, 12). Both the Jews and the general population of Susa celebrate Mordecai’s new prominence and his countermeasure (vv. 15–17).

**8:1 On that day.** Seemingly the same day that had begun with the king’s sleeplessness (6:1).

**gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman.** According to Persian custom, the property of a traitor (“house” implies all his possessions) is confiscated by the crown. Here Esther receives compensation for the wrong done to her.

**Mordecai came before the king.** Mordecai is given official status (see 1:14) and effectively takes over Haman’s official and personal position.
In her second appeal to Ahasuerus, Esther abandons her cool, calculating approach, and resorts to emotional entreaty.

Esther presents her case carefully and with a liberal dose of flattery. Two of the conditional clauses relate to the king’s assessment of the situation and two to his personal regard for Esther, which is in reality the only leverage she has with him.

verse_quote: But you may write as you please.
note: The “you” is emphatic. Ahasuerus does not want to think through the details of rectifying the situation. Typically he delegates others to act in his name with full authority.

The new decree, issued two months and ten days after the first (3:12), is almost identical to Haman’s first decree (3:12–15). The date is June 25, 474 B.C. There are still eight months and twenty days to go until Haman’s decree will take effect. It cannot be formally revoked, but Mordecai’s strategy nullifies its effect by permitting the Jews to defend themselves.

**8:9 and also to the Jews.** An addition to the original decree to ensure that the Jews knew they could take appropriate action.
The additional details regarding the speed and reliability with which the second decree is to be conveyed indicate the urgency of the situation (see v. 14).

verse_quote: to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate.
note:
Repeats the terms of the original decree (3:13).

**children and women included.** While this might relate to the families of their attackers, it is more probable that it again repeats the language of 3:13 and refers to the families of the Jews.

verse_quote: to take vengeance on their enemies.
note: Retaliation is authorized to punish any who take action against the Jews. Those who act on the basis of Haman’s edict will share his fate.

Whereas after the first edict Mordecai had torn his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes (4:1), the situation is now completely reversed, and he is dressed with regal splendor, and not just for a single parade (see 6:11). Blue and white are Persian royal colors. The majority reaction in the city shows that anti-Jewish feeling is not widespread throughout the population.

verse_quote: many from the peoples ... declared themselves Jews.
note: The conversion of those from other nations who fear the Jews marks a climax in the story (see Josh. 2:9; Ex. 15:14–16; Ps. 105:38).

The day set for the implementation of Haman’s decree, March 7, 473 B.C. (see 3:13), arrives. Despite the promulgation of countermeasures, some still attack the Jews. In Susa, five hundred enemies are killed (v. 12), and at Esther’s request the action is continued for another day, which leads to three hundred more deaths (vv. 13–15). Throughout the provinces of the empire, many who attack the Jews are slain, but the Jews refrain from plundering their property.

**9:1 the reverse occurred.** The theme of ironic reversal is again emphasized. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

Fear of the God of the Jews is behind the Persians’ pervasive fear of the Jews (see Ex. 15:14–16). The reversal (v. 1 note) is so complete that all the officials who were to have enforced the extermination of the Jews now aid them. They are acutely aware of who has come to enjoy royal favor.

The extent of the killing is emphasized (vv. 6–11), but so is the Jews’ not plundering their enemies (v. 10). Their refusal to plunder recalls the plundering of the Amalekites that led to Saul’s demise (1 Sam. 15:17–19). This contrast (see 8:11) suggests the propriety of their conduct in this final encounter with the Amalekites, despite the extent of the killing. It seems that the Jews are acting in accordance with the rules pertaining to a war of the Lord (Num. 31:1 note; Josh. 6:17).

verse_quote: but they laid no hand on the plunder.
note: This significant detail is repeated in vv. 15, 16 to emphasize the restraint that the Jews exercise. It is a deliberate decision not to enrich themselves at the expense of their enemies.

Esther’s requests for further vengeance (v. 13), which may be due to widespread anti-Jewish sentiment in the city, leads to a second day of bloodshed in Susa (v. 15). Notably, the emphasis in the narrative is on killing enemies, not just on winning a victory. Esther is operating in accordance with the directives applicable to a war of the Lord (see Josh. 8:29; 10:26).

verse_quote: the ten sons of Haman were hanged.
note: The bodies of the dead sons (v. 12) are displayed as a warning and a sign of ultimate dishonor (2:23 note).

The slaughter of a further seventy-five thousand enemies emphasizes the extent of the antagonism toward the Jews throughout the empire, which in turn explains the celebrations that follow.

**relief from their enemies.** The rest granted to the Jews at this time becomes the basis for the annual celebration of Purim (also v. 22). Such rest was earlier closely associated with blotting out the memory of the Amalekites (Deut. 25:19).

The difference of the day on which the feast of Purim is held is first explained (vv. 17–19). The further record (vv. 20–32) shows how important it is to the writer to establish that Purim is to be celebrated by each new generation of Jews. There is no mention of God. The feast is based on the edict of Mordecai and Esther (v. 31).

The additional day of bloodshed in the capital leads to two different dates for the observance of Purim. It is still the case that the Jews celebrate it on the fifteenth in Jerusalem, but on the fourteenth elsewhere.

verse_quote: send gifts of food to one another.
note: The exchange of gifts, usually food (v. 22), enables even the poorest Jew to join in the celebrations (Deut. 16:11, 14; Neh. 8:10, 12) and is a further instance of providential care for the oppressed, here within the Jewish community itself.
He does this by incorporating the information in the letters of instruction he sends regarding the festival.

This brief summary of the events of the preceding chapters focuses, not on Esther and Mordecai, but on the king and Haman, and pre­sents Haman as the archetypal adversary of all Jews, past and present (3:10; 8:1; 9:10)., 25
A plural form of _pur_, a Babylonian term for “lot” (see 3:7).

Esther along with Mordecai sends a final official letter regarding Purim that carefully places the feast within the setting of the more established Israelite practices of fasting and lamentation (v. 31). In this way, Purim is made an official religious celebration of the Jews, a task the writer of Esther seems to view as important because of the non-Mosaic origin of the feast.

The epilogue mirrors the introductory statements about the reign of Ahasuerus (1:1, 2). Though the Lord granted the Jews relief from impending annihilation, the political structures of the world continue to dominate their lives. The salvation of God’s people is not yet complete, even though they now have a powerful advocate in the royal court. True deliverance awaits the coming of one able to do far more than Esther and Mordecai.

**10:1** The extent of Ahasuerus’s power is brought out by his ability to impose taxation throughout his land empire and on the cities of the eastern Mediterranean, such as those of the Phoenicians, whose economies were based on maritime trade.

The historicity of the narrative is emphasized by citing Persian official records as sources of further information about Ahasuerus and the status he conferred on Mordecai, who continued to work within the official structures of the empire. For some reason, Esther’s name is not included in the postscript.

Mordecai is esteemed as an ideal Jewish statesman, recalling the status of Joseph (Gen. 41:40) and Daniel (Dan. 2:48; 5:29; 6:28). His importance as a model for the Jews and in the establishment of Purim is acknowledged in the apocryphal book of Maccabees, where Purim is called “the day before Mordecai’s day” (2 Macc. 15:36).
